items.q: My grandmother (A) has lived in this village for forty years before she (B) finally moved to the city (C) to be closer to (D) her grandchildren.
items.explanation: An action completed before another past action (she moved) takes the past perfect: had lived, not the present perfect.

items.q: The number of students (A) who take part in the science fair every year (B) have grown steadily (C) since the school (D) built its new laboratory.
items.explanation: The subject is the number (singular), so the verb must be singular: has grown. Only a number of takes a plural verb.

items.q: My uncle, (A) who has worked in Da Nang for twenty years, (B) believes that (C) a honest worker is always (D) respected by his colleagues.
items.explanation: The article depends on the sound, not the letter: honest begins with a vowel sound (the h is silent), so it takes an.

items.q: The teacher (A) was pleased with our presentation, but she (B) reminded us that we (C) still needed to pay more attention (D) on spelling.
items.explanation: The fixed expression is pay attention to something; on is not used after attention.

items.q: The (A) succeed of the school football team this season (B) has surprised everyone, (C) especially the coach, who (D) expected a difficult year.
items.explanation: After the and before of a noun is needed: success. Succeed is the verb form.

items.q: (A) Last month, Lan and (B) me were chosen to represent our school at a (C) national speaking contest, (D) which was held in Hue in early June.
items.explanation: Lan and ... is the subject of were chosen, so the subject pronoun I is required, not the object pronoun me.

items.q: Mount Fansipan is (A) known as the highest peak in Vietnam, (B) but it is not (C) as high than the great mountains (D) of the Himalayas.
items.explanation: An equal (or negative equal) comparison uses as + adjective + as; than only follows a comparative such as higher.

items.q: If you (A) heat ice, it (B) turns into water, (C) and if you keep heating it, it (D) would become steam.
options: and if you keep heating it
items.explanation: This is a real condition about a scientific fact, so the result clause takes will (or the present simple), not the unreal would.

items.q: The tour guide (A) told to us that the ancient temple (B) had been built more than (C) six hundred years earlier by (D) a powerful king.
items.explanation: In reported speech tell takes a direct object with no preposition: told us that. It is said to us but told us.

items.q: The old man (A) who lives next door has a dog (B) which name is Lucky, and (C) it barks at (D) anyone passing the gate.
items.explanation: Possession inside a relative clause (the dog's name) is expressed with whose; which cannot stand before a noun like this.

items.q: Nobody in the office (A) seemed to know (B) exactly (C) where was the manager, so the visitors (D) had to wait outside for nearly an hour.
items.explanation: An embedded (indirect) question keeps statement order, subject before verb: where the manager was, with no inversion.

items.q: Before the marathon, the runners (A) were advised to drink plenty of water, (B) get enough sleep and (C) avoid (D) doing any mistakes with their diet.
items.explanation: The collocation is make a mistake, never do a mistake. The -ing form after avoid is correct.

items.q: (A) Much people believe that robots (B) will take over most factory jobs, (C) but experts say new kinds of work (D) will appear as well.
items.explanation: People is a plural countable noun, so it takes many; much is used only with uncountable nouns.

items.q: The final match (A) went ahead as planned (B) despite it was raining heavily, and (C) both teams played well until the (D) last minute.
items.explanation: Despite is a preposition and must be followed by a noun or -ing form (despite the heavy rain); a full clause with a subject and verb needs although.

items.q: While I (A) was doing my homework last night, the electricity (B) suddenly went off and I (C) am sitting in the dark (D) for nearly an hour.
items.explanation: The whole story happened last night, so the completed action must be in the past simple: sat, not the present continuous.

items.q: Each of the twelve paintings (A) in the exhibition (B) was created by a local artist, and (C) the money raised (D) go to the children's hospital.
items.explanation: Money is an uncountable, singular subject, so its verb takes -s: the money raised goes. Each of + singular verb in (B) is correct.

items.q: (A) A Moon travels around the Earth (B) once every twenty-seven days, (C) which is why we see (D) different shapes of it during a month.
items.explanation: Unique things in our world (the Moon, the Earth, the Sun) take the definite article because there is only one of them.

items.q: My younger brother is (A) very good at maths, but he (B) is afraid from speaking (C) in front of a large audience, (D) even his classmates.
items.explanation: The adjective afraid is followed by of (afraid of speaking / afraid of dogs); from is a Vietnamese-style transfer error.

items.q: Scientists (A) have discovered that some birds can fly (B) thousands of kilometres (C) without stop, using the stars (D) to find their way at night.
items.explanation: After a preposition such as without a verb must take the -ing form: without stopping.

items.q: The twins (A) look so alike that even their teachers (B) sometimes confuse them, (C) although they themselves (D) find easy to tell each other apart.
items.explanation: With find/think/make + adjective + to-infinitive the empty pronoun it is required as the object: find it easy to tell.

items.q: (A) The more hard you practise the piano, (B) the better you will play, (C) but you should also rest your hands (D) between sessions.
items.explanation: Hard is a one-syllable adverb, so its comparative is harder; the double comparative pattern is The harder ..., the better ....

items.q: If I (A) were you, I (B) will apologise to Minh (C) before the end of the day, (D) because he still looks upset.
options: before the end of the day
items.explanation: If I were you is a second (unreal) conditional, so the main clause needs would + bare infinitive, not will.

items.q: At the interview, the manager (A) asked me (B) politely (C) why did I want the job and (D) what my strengths were.
options: why did I want the job
items.explanation: A reported question drops the auxiliary did and uses statement order with the verb shifted back: why I wanted. Segment (D) shows the correct pattern.

items.q: The bridge (A) that connects the two halves of the town (B) was built in 1932, (C) and it is still used by (D) people who they cross the river every day.
options: and it is still used by
items.explanation: The relative pronoun who is already the subject of cross, so a second subject they must not be repeated in the clause.

items.q: My father (A) drives always carefully on the motorway, (B) even when the road is empty, (C) because he once saw (D) a serious accident there.
options: even when the road is empty
items.explanation: Adverbs of frequency such as always go before a main verb (but after be): always drives.

items.q: Our teacher (A) encouraged us to (B) make a research on local plants (C) before writing our reports, (D) so we visited the park twice.
items.explanation: Research is uncountable and collocates with do (do research / carry out research); make a research is not English.

items.q: There (A) were so many visitors at the festival that the organisers had (B) to borrow (C) a little extra chairs (D) from the nearby school.
items.explanation: Chairs is a plural countable noun, so it takes a few; a little goes only with uncountable nouns (a little water).

items.q: Both the museum (A) and the library (B) are closed on Mondays, (C) so we will have to visit them (D) either on Tuesday and Wednesday.
items.explanation: The paired conjunction is either ... or; and pairs with both, as in segment (A), not with either.

items.q: Since the new motorway (A) opens last year, the journey to my grandparents' house (B) has taken only half an hour (C) instead of (D) nearly two.
items.explanation: Last year is a finished past time, so the verb must be past simple: opened. The present perfect in (B) after since is correct.

items.q: Astronauts on the space station (A) must exercise for two hours every day, (B) otherwise their muscles (C) can to become weak (D) in the absence of gravity.
items.explanation: Modal verbs (can, must, should) are followed by the bare infinitive without to: can become.
